tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

# Brass: the editing reference, compact

Brass is written by models and reviewed by people. The facts a reviewer needs sit in declarations: what a function may reach, what it requires, what it promises. Plan an edit from declarations; open a body only when they do not say what you need. When you change a type or refinement, find every declaration that uses it; a refinement shared by two functions changes both. Open `system.brass` when an entry point's access parameters change.

**What checks your work in this run.** Nothing compiles, checks, or runs. Your patch is evaluated after you finish.

## Sentences, not words

| Shape | Means | Inside it |
|---|---|---|
| `type T = B where <condition>` | the values of `B` that pass the condition | `it` is the value; its fields are `it.field` |
| `fn f(params) -> T` then `before`, `after`, `example` | an operation and its obligations | `before` names parameters; `after` adds `result` |
| `if x is T then … else …` | a test that picks a branch | inside `then`, `x` counts as a `T` |
| `for x in xs` | a bounded loop | `x` is one element; `break` leaves |
| `any x in xs where cond` / `all x in xs where cond` | is at least one / every element like this? | no effects; `any` of empty is `false`, **`all` of empty is `true`** |
| `r with { field: v }` | a copy of `r` with fields changed | other fields carry over |
| `r with { status enters S }` | a copy of `r` in state `S` | only a declared edge is legal; the `when` fields of `S` must be given |
| `access A` then `allow op(…)` | an outside capability and what it offers | reached only through a parameter of type `A` |

`in` asks membership or walks a collection; `is` asks a type or an `Ok`/`Err` arm. `where` states a condition; `if` chooses. `with` changes fields; `enters` changes state along a declared edge. `after` is proven for every input; `example` is one input, tested.

## Modules

```brass
# ship/shipments.brass
module ship.shipments
import ship.ids as ids

interface
  type Weight   = Int where it in 1 to 50000
  type Shipment = { id: ids.ShipmentId, weight: Weight, fragile: Bool, status: ShipmentStatus }
  fn grams_over(s: Shipment, ceiling: Weight) -> Int
    after result == s.weight - ceiling
private
  fn is_heavy(s: Shipment) -> Bool
body
  fn grams_over(s, ceiling) = s.weight - ceiling
  fn is_heavy(s) = s.weight >= 20000
```

- One module per file: `interface` (public), optional `private`, then `body`. Write `interface` and `body` even when empty. A function is declared once with types; its body repeats the names without types. A body with no declaration, or a declaration with no body, is a rejection.
- Every import has an alias and every imported name goes through it: `ids.ShipmentId`, never `ShipmentId`. No two imports share an alias; imports do not cycle. No versions on `module` or `import`.
- `type ShipmentId = Text` names an existing type. `Text` has `length`: `type Note = Text where it.length in 1 to 200`.
- Types and constructors start uppercase, everything else lowercase. Keywords are never names (not `to`, not `in`). `system`, `requires`, `grants`, `limit` are keywords only in the system file.
- A declaration continues onto the next line while a `(`, `<`, or `{` it opened is still open, as in Python; indentation inside does not matter.
- A record literal names every field: `{ id: id, weight: w, fragile: false, status: ShipmentStatus.Packed }`.
- **Authority is a parameter.** A function reaches outside only through an access it was handed. No access parameter, no effect.

## Conditions

```brass
type Ready = Shipment where it.status in {ShipmentStatus.Packed}
type Route = { origin: ids.Depot, dest: ids.Depot } where it.origin != it.dest
type Batch = Array<Shipment> where it.length in 0 to 200
type HeavyReady = Ready where it.weight >= 20000
```

- `it` is the value, and its fields are `it.field`, nesting by dots. A bare field name is a rejection: write `it.status`, not `status`. A refinement may follow a type anywhere a type is written. A refined value passes where its base is expected; a base value does not pass where the refinement is expected.
- Tests: `x in 1 to 10` (range), `x in {A, B}` (set), `x in s` (a named set), `x is T` (refinement; `x` must have `T`'s fields), `x is Ok` / `x is Err`. A state test is a set test: `s.status in {ShipmentStatus.Packed}`. `x is None` is a rejection: write `x == None`.
- A passed test narrows the name inside `then`; tests joined with `and` all narrow; `or` narrows nothing; `not` narrows nothing. In `else`, only a single test on states or on `Ok`/`Err` knows the complement. A narrowing lasts until the name is rebound.
- **Only `x is T` gives a value a named type.** Testing a field (`p.status in {…}`) lets you read what depends on it but does not make `p` a `Ready`. A `let`, argument, field, or result also holds a refinement when the checker can prove its condition there from the facts that establish a `before` (see Types and literals). A literal, a `const` name, or a `with` whose fields the checker sees satisfies a refinement directly when the condition holds.

**Contracts.**

```brass
fn postage(s: Heavy, base: Cents) -> Cents
  before base <= 1000
  after  result == base + 500
  example postage({ id: "s1", weight: 25000, fragile: false, status: ShipmentStatus.Packed }, 400) == 900
```

- `before`: what the caller must establish, by a parameter's type, a `const` fact, its own `before`, a callee's `after`, or a test on the path. `after`: what holds on success; on `Outcome<T>` it speaks of the value inside `Ok`, named `result`. Several `before` lines hold together.
- A condition may use `+`, `-`, `*` by a constant or of bounded values, `/` and `%` by a nonzero constant, comparisons, `in`, `not`, `and`, `or`, parameters, `result`, fields, `const` names, `length`. No calls, no quantifiers, no floats. "When p then q" is `not (p) or q`. At one level of parentheses use `and` or `or`, never both. The left side of `and` holds while the right is checked.
- A caller's clause that depends on a callee with no contract cannot be proven: the remedy is a contract on the callee.
- `example f(args) == value`: one concrete call, run by `check`. Only on a total `fn` with no access parameter; the arguments must satisfy the types and every `before`. Tested, never proven.
- **Tiers.** Proven: every contract on a Brass function, unless it is proved from an enforced fact. Enforced by the runtime: an access's reserved bounds and authority checks, every reply from outside, an entry point's parameter types and `before` lines at the boundary. Assumed: nothing checks it. Only proven is a guarantee.

## Bodies

A body is lines run top to bottom; the last line is the value. `and`/`or` stop at the first operand that decides them.

```brass
fn total_weight(batch) =
  let total: Int = 0
  for s in batch
    total = total + s.weight
  total
```

- Every `let` names its type. An unread `let`, or a value computed and dropped (unless it is `Done`, as in `store.save(x)?` on its own line), is a rejection. Parameters and loop variables cannot be rebound. A branch that does not rebind a name leaves its old value. Rebinding gives the name a new value; the old value is unchanged, as every value is.
- `if c then a else b` is a value (both branches); `if c then x = x + 1` on its own line is a step and needs no `else`. A branch may be an indented block whose last line is its value.
- **Failure.** A function that can fail returns `Outcome<T>` (`Ok(T) | Err(FailureCode, Text)`); nothing else marks it. `Outcome<Done>` and `Ok(Done)` for no value. `Err` always carries a code (`Unauthorized InvalidInput Conflict Unavailable ResourceExhausted Other NotFound`; `Unknown` is the runtime's, never written) and a text. `x?` yields the value inside `Ok` or returns the `Err` to the caller there; legal only in a function that returns `Outcome`. To replace a failure, test `x is Err` first, then `?` in the `Ok` branch cannot fail. A last line `call()` returns its `Outcome` as is; `call()?` as the whole last line is a rejection. A body cannot read which code an `Err` holds. An `Err` undoes nothing: effects already made through an access stand, so check what can refuse before you act. A retry loop retries every failure; retry only what is safe to repeat.
- **Maybe.** `Maybe<T>` holds a `T` or `None`; the caller passes the value itself or `None`. Inside `if x != None then …`, `x` is a plain `T`; the `else` of either test knows the other. No `Maybe<Maybe<T>>`. `Maybe` for normal absence; `Err(NotFound, …)` for failure.
- **No early exit, so tests nest.** Name cheap facts with `let`, decide, and put a lookup with `?` after the tests that decide whether it is needed:

```brass
fn dispatch(carrier, store, id, region) =
  let s: shipments.Shipment = store.shipment(id)?
  if s is shipments.Ready then
    let cleared: Bool = if region in {ids.Region.Abroad} then store.customs_cleared(s.id)? else true
    if cleared then
      let t: ids.TrackingId = carrier.book(s, region)?
      store.save(shipments.ship(s, t))
    else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "customs has not cleared this shipment")
  else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "shipment is not packed")
```

- Negate with `not`; `not a == b` is `not (a == b)`.
- **Loops are bounded.** `for` walks a range (`for i in 1 to 3`; `i` is known in range) or an array whose type bounds its length. A loop from `[]` appending at most one element per source element keeps the source's bound. `break` leaves the nearest enclosing loop, and the body continues after it. `lo to hi` includes both ends: `1 to 3` runs three times. No `while`, `return`, recursion, or `match`. Arrays cannot be indexed; walk them.
- **`any`/`all`** are `Bool`; the predicate is total and effect-free (no `?`, no access call), sees surrounding names, runs to the end of the expression (parenthesize to combine), body only.

**Arrays and sets.** An array cannot be indexed: walk it with `for`, test it with `any`/`all`, measure it with `length`, extend it with `++` (`xs ++ [x]`). There is no `in` on an array value; membership is `any y in xs where y == x`. A `Set<T>` is for bounds and `in` only (`x in {A, B}`, `region in regions`); `{a, b}` is its literal, and it is not iterable. To find the element at a position, count in a loop:

```brass
let at: Int = 0
for l in ls
  at = at + 1
  if at == pos then picked = picked ++ [l]
```

**Several `when` fields.** A record may carry several conditional fields, testing one machine field or different ones. Each conditional field carries its own `when`.

```brass
type Order = { id: ids.OrderId, status: OrderStatus,
               tracking:  ids.TrackingId when it.status in {OrderStatus.Shipped, OrderStatus.Delivered},
               signed_by: ids.Badge      when it.status in {OrderStatus.Delivered},
               signed_at: Int            when it.status in {OrderStatus.Delivered} }
```

## Records and states

```brass
machine ShipmentStatus
  states  Packed, Shipped, Arrived, Returned
  initial Packed
  Packed  enters Shipped
  Shipped enters Arrived | Returned

type Shipment = { id: ids.ShipmentId, weight: Weight, fragile: Bool, status: ShipmentStatus,
                  tracking: ids.TrackingId when it.status in {ShipmentStatus.Shipped, ShipmentStatus.Arrived} }

fn ship(s: Ready, t: ids.TrackingId) -> Shipment
fn ship(s, t) = s with { status enters ShipmentStatus.Shipped, tracking: t }
```

- `with { … }` copies a record and replaces named fields; a repeated or unknown field, or an empty `with { }`, is a rejection. A `with` that changes none of the fields a refinement tests keeps that refinement: a note added to a `Ready` shipment is still `Ready`. Changing a field that a refinement tests, `enters` included, gives back the base type.
- A state change is `status enters S` inside `with`; a plain `status: S` there is a rejection. A `with` that does not name the state keeps it. `enters` names one state; branch to choose. The checker must know every possible current state has an edge to the target. A literal may hold the initial state, or a state obtained legitimately; inventing a later state in a literal is a rejection.
- A `when` field exists only in the listed states; the field it tests is itself unconditional, and its type is a named type: read it only where the state is known; the update entering those states supplies it; a move between listed states keeps it; the update leaving them drops it, and naming it there is a rejection.

**A field for states of several machines takes a shared vocabulary.**

A field has one machine type, and no type means "a state of one of these machines". When one record must hold states from several machines, declare a shared vocabulary of state names and one converter per machine, and convert where you build the record:

```brass
# ship/log.brass
type Subject = Shipment | Pickup
type Step    = Packed | Shipped | Arrived | Returned | Booked | Collected | Missed
type Entry   = { subject: Subject, subject_id: Text, was: Step, now: Step }

fn of_shipment(s: shipments.ShipmentStatus) -> Step
  example of_shipment(shipments.ShipmentStatus.Arrived) == Step.Arrived
fn of_pickup(p: pickups.PickupStatus) -> Step
  example of_pickup(pickups.PickupStatus.Missed) == Step.Missed
```

- A field that held one machine's state now holds the vocabulary. A `subject` beside a neutral id says which machine a value came from.
- Write a direct `example` for each state; each one is checked.
- Widening the field to `Text`, or adding a second record or host operation for the second machine, is legal and loses what the type said.

## Accesses and the system file

```brass
access Carrier { regions: Set<ids.Region>, budget_calls: Int }
  allow book(s: shipments.Ready, region: ids.Region) -> Outcome<ids.TrackingId>
    before region in regions and s.weight <= 50000
access Store
  allow shipment(id: ids.ShipmentId) -> Outcome<shipments.Shipment>
  allow save(s: shipments.Shipment) -> Outcome<Done>
```

- An `access` is a declaration in `interface` or `private`. A body calls through its parameter: `carrier.book(s, region)`. Every `allow` returns `Outcome<T>`. A `before` on an `allow` splits by conjunct: one naming a bound is an authority check the runtime enforces; any other is a contract the caller proves. An `after` on an `allow` is checked on every successful reply. `budget_<unit>` and `deadline_ms` are reserved bounds; a bare `budget` is a rejection. - **Settling.** When Finance pays an expense report, they may settle it against one of the staff member's paid advances: the report's payment is reduced by the advance. - **Budget.** An advance counts against its department's budget for its period while Approved or Paid. Once settled it stops counting, since the report it was settled against counts instead.

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

```markdown
---
name: {{short-kebab-case-slug}}
description: {{one-line summary, used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
metadata:

---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].}}

- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated

- If the memory names a function or flag: grep for it.
- If the user is about to act on your recommendation (not just asking about history), verify first.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- Agents run in the background by default. When an agent runs in the background, you will be automatically notified when it completes — do NOT sleep, poll, or proactively check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user instead.
- **Foreground vs background**: Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — e.g., a research agent whose finding gates the edit you're about to make. Otherwise let it run in the background (the default) — this includes fire-and-forget work, independent investigations, and anything where the user might hand you something else in the meantime. Wanting the result "next" is not enough on its own.
- **Don't race**: after launching a background agent, you know nothing about its results. Never fabricate or predict them in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The completion notification arrives in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks before it lands, say the agent is still running — give status, not a guess.
- To continue a previously spawned agent, use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name as the `to` field — that resumes it with full context. A new Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs (except subagent_type: "fork"), so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch both a build-validator agent and a test-runner agent in parallel, send a single message with both tool calls.
- With `isolation: "worktree"`, the worktree is automatically cleaned up if the agent makes no changes; otherwise the path and branch are returned in the result.

## When to fork

Fork yourself (pass `subagent_type: "fork"`) when the intermediate tool output isn't worth keeping in your context. The criterion is qualitative — "will I need this output again" — not task size. Fork open-ended questions. If research can be broken into independent questions, launch parallel forks in one message. A fork beats a fresh subagent for this — it inherits context and shares your cache.

Forks are cheap because they share your prompt cache.

**Don't peek.** A background fork's tool result includes an `output_file` path — do not Read or tail it. It sends a completion notification; trust it. Reading the transcript mid-flight pulls the fork's tool noise into your context, which defeats the point of forking.

**Don't race.** After launching a background fork, you know nothing about what it found. Never fabricate or predict fork results in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The notification arrives as a user-role message in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks a follow-up before the notification lands, tell them the fork is still running — give status, not a guess.

**Writing a fork prompt.** Since the fork inherits your context, the prompt is a *directive* — what to do, not what the situation is. Be specific about scope: what's in, what's out, what another agent is handling. Don't re-explain background.


## Writing the prompt

Any agent other than a fork starts with zero context. Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").
- Lookups: hand over the exact command. Investigations: hand over the question — prescribed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.

For fresh agents, terse command-style prompts produce shallow, generic work.

**Never delegate understanding.** Don't write "based on your findings, fix the bug" or "based on the research, implement it." Those phrases push synthesis onto the agent instead of doing it yourself. Write prompts that prove you understood: include file paths, line numbers, what specifically to change.

Example usage:

<example>
user: "What's left on this branch before we can ship?"
assistant: <thinking>Forking this — it's a survey question. I want the punch list, not the git output in my context.</thinking>
Agent({
  subagent_type: "fork",
  name: "ship-audit",
  description: "Branch ship-readiness audit",
  prompt: "Audit what's left before this branch can ship. Check: uncommitted changes, commits ahead of main, whether tests exist, whether the GrowthBook gate is wired up, whether CI-relevant files changed. Report a punch list — done vs. missing. Under 200 words."
})
assistant: Ship-readiness audit running.
<commentary>
Turn ends here. The coordinator knows nothing about the findings yet. What follows is a SEPARATE turn — the notification arrives from outside, as a user-role message. It is not something the coordinator writes.
</commentary>
[later turn — notification arrives as user message]
assistant: Audit's back. Three blockers: no tests for the new prompt path, GrowthBook gate wired but not in build_flags.yaml, and one uncommitted file.
</example>

<example>
user: "so is the gate wired up or not"
<commentary>
User asks mid-wait. The audit fork was launched to answer exactly this, and it hasn't returned. The coordinator does not have this answer. Give status, not a fabricated result.
</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.
</example>

<example>
user: "Can you get a second opinion on whether this migration is safe?"
assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>
<commentary>
A non-fork subagent_type is specified, so the agent starts fresh. It needs full context in the prompt. The briefing explains what to assess and why.
</commentary>
Agent({
  name: "migration-review",
  description: "Independent migration review",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
  prompt: "Review migration 0042_user_schema.sql for safety. Context: we're adding a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table. Existing rows get a backfill default. I want a second opinion on whether the backfill approach is safe under concurrent writes — I've checked locking behavior but want independent verification. Report: is this safe, and if not, what specifically breaks?"
})
</example>

**Writing a fork prompt.** Since the fork inherits your context, the prompt is a *directive* — what to do, not what the situation is. Be specific about scope: what's in, what's out, what another agent is handling. Don't re-explain background.


## Writing the prompt

Any agent other than a fork starts with zero context. Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").

user: "so is the gate wired up or not"

</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.

assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>

tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
 - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not read the file first.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

5	
6	interface
7	  type VendorId     = Text
8	  type PoId         = Text
9	  type TxnId        = Text
10	  type DelegationId = Text
11	  type CostCenterId = Text
12	  type EntityId     = Text
13	  type Region       = Island | Mainland | Offsite
14	  type Vehicle      = Car | Truck | Boat
15	  type Amount       = Int where it in 1 to 1000000000
16	
17	  machine PoStatus
18	    states  Requested, Approved, Rejected, Received, Closed
19	    initial Requested
20	    Requested enters Approved | Rejected
21	    Approved  enters Received
22	    Received  enters Closed
23	
24	  machine CardStatus
25	    states  Open, Matched, Disputed
26	    initial Open
27	    Open     enters Matched | Disputed
28	    Disputed enters Open
29	
30	  type Vendor        = { id: VendorId, name: Text, active: Bool }
31	  type PurchaseOrder = { id: PoId, vendor: VendorId, requested_by: ids.Badge, department: ids.DepartmentId, period: ids.Period, amount: Amount, status: PoStatus, approvals: reports.Approvals, received: ids.Money }
32	  type POs           = Array<PurchaseOrder> where it.length in 0 to 1000
33	  type PoRequested   = PurchaseOrder where it.status in {PoStatus.Requested}
34	  type PoApproved    = PurchaseOrder where it.status in {PoStatus.Approved}
35	  type PoReceived    = PurchaseOrder where it.status in {PoStatus.Received}
36	
37	  type CardTxn  = { id: TxnId, badge: ids.Badge, period: ids.Period, amount: Amount, category: ids.Category, merchant: ids.Description, status: CardStatus, matched: Maybe<ids.ReportId> }
38	  type Txns     = Array<CardTxn> where it.length in 0 to 1000
39	  type OpenTxn  = CardTxn where it.status in {CardStatus.Open}
40	
41	  type Delegation  = { id: DelegationId, delegator: ids.Badge, delegate: ids.Badge, first: ids.Period, last: ids.Period, revoked: Bool }
42	  type Delegations = Array<Delegation> where it.length in 0 to 100
43	
44	  type CostCenter = { id: CostCenterId, entity: EntityId, name: Text }
45	  type Entity     = { id: EntityId, name: Text }
46	  type DeptIds    = Array<ids.DepartmentId> where it.length in 0 to 50
47	  type CardLimit  = { badge: ids.Badge, limit: ids.Money }
48	  type ExceptionId = Text
49	
50	  machine ExceptionStatus
51	    states  Pending, Granted, Denied
52	    initial Pending
53	    Pending enters Granted | Denied
54	
55	  type PolicyException = { id: ExceptionId, report: ids.ReportId, position: Int, badge: ids.Badge, reason: ids.Reason, status: ExceptionStatus, decided_by: Maybe<ids.Badge> }
56	  type Exceptions      = Array<PolicyException> where it.length in 0 to 50
57	  type PendingException = PolicyException where it.status in {ExceptionStatus.Pending}
58	  type Badges     = Array<ids.Badge> where it.length in 0 to 1000
59	
60	  fn commitments(pos: POs) -> Int
61	    after result >= 0
62	  fn in_force(d: Delegation, period: ids.Period) -> Bool
63	    example in_force({ id: "d", delegator: "a", delegate: "b", first: 2, last: 4, revoked: false }, 4) == true
64	    example in_force({ id: "d", delegator: "a", delegate: "b", first: 2, last: 4, revoked: true }, 3) == false
65	  fn per_diem_rate(r: Region) -> Int
66	    example per_diem_rate(Region.Offsite) == 12000
67	  fn mileage_rate(v: Vehicle) -> Int

# desk/records.brass
module desk.records
import desk.ids as ids
import desk.reports as reports

interface
  type VendorId     = Text
  type PoId         = Text
  type TxnId        = Text
  type DelegationId = Text
  type CostCenterId = Text
  type EntityId     = Text
  type Region       = Island | Mainland | Offsite
  type Vehicle      = Car | Truck | Boat
  type Amount       = Int where it in 1 to 1000000000

  machine PoStatus
    states  Requested, Approved, Rejected, Received, Closed
    initial Requested
    Requested enters Approved | Rejected
    Approved  enters Received
    Received  enters Closed

  machine CardStatus
    states  Open, Matched, Disputed
    initial Open
    Open     enters Matched | Disputed
    Disputed enters Open

  type Vendor        = { id: VendorId, name: Text, active: Bool }
  type PurchaseOrder = { id: PoId, vendor: VendorId, requested_by: ids.Badge, department: ids.DepartmentId, period: ids.Period, amount: Amount, status: PoStatus, approvals: reports.Approvals, received: ids.Money }
  type POs           = Array<PurchaseOrder> where it.length in 0 to 1000
  type PoRequested   = PurchaseOrder where it.status in {PoStatus.Requested}
  type PoApproved    = PurchaseOrder where it.status in {PoStatus.Approved}
  type PoReceived    = PurchaseOrder where it.status in {PoStatus.Received}

  type CardTxn  = { id: TxnId, badge: ids.Badge, period: ids.Period, amount: Amount, category: ids.Category, merchant: ids.Description, status: CardStatus, matched: Maybe<ids.ReportId> }
  type Txns     = Array<CardTxn> where it.length in 0 to 1000
  type OpenTxn  = CardTxn where it.status in {CardStatus.Open}

  type Delegation  = { id: DelegationId, delegator: ids.Badge, delegate: ids.Badge, first: ids.Period, last: ids.Period, revoked: Bool }
  type Delegations = Array<Delegation> where it.length in 0 to 100

  type CostCenter = { id: CostCenterId, entity: EntityId, name: Text }
  type Entity     = { id: EntityId, name: Text }
  type DeptIds    = Array<ids.DepartmentId> where it.length in 0 to 50
  type CardLimit  = { badge: ids.Badge, limit: ids.Money }
  type ExceptionId = Text

  machine ExceptionStatus
    states  Pending, Granted, Denied
    initial Pending
    Pending enters Granted | Denied

  type PolicyException = { id: ExceptionId, report: ids.ReportId, position: Int, badge: ids.Badge, reason: ids.Reason, status: ExceptionStatus, decided_by: Maybe<ids.Badge> }
  type Exceptions      = Array<PolicyException> where it.length in 0 to 50
  type PendingException = PolicyException where it.status in {ExceptionStatus.Pending}
  type Badges     = Array<ids.Badge> where it.length in 0 to 1000

  fn commitments(pos: POs) -> Int
    after result >= 0
  fn in_force(d: Delegation, period: ids.Period) -> Bool
    example in_force({ id: "d", delegator: "a", delegate: "b", first: 2, last: 4, revoked: false }, 4) == true
    example in_force({ id: "d", delegator: "a", delegate: "b", first: 2, last: 4, revoked: true }, 3) == false
  fn per_diem_rate(r: Region) -> Int
    example per_diem_rate(Region.Offsite) == 12000
  fn mileage_rate(v: Vehicle) -> Int
    example mileage_rate(Vehicle.Boat) == 250

  fn add_po_approval(po: PoRequested, who: ids.Badge) -> PurchaseOrder
    before po.approvals.length < 2
  fn approve_po(po: PoRequested) -> PurchaseOrder
  fn reject_po(po: PoRequested) -> PurchaseOrder
  fn receive_po(po: PoApproved, received: ids.Money) -> PurchaseOrder
  fn close_po(po: PoReceived) -> PurchaseOrder
  fn decide(e: PendingException, grant: Bool, by: ids.Badge) -> PolicyException
  fn match_txn(t: OpenTxn, report: ids.ReportId) -> CardTxn
  fn dispute_txn(t: OpenTxn) -> CardTxn
body
  fn commitments(pos) =
    let sum: Int = 0
    for p in pos
      if p.status in {PoStatus.Approved} then sum = sum + p.amount
      else if p.status in {PoStatus.Received, PoStatus.Closed} then sum = sum + p.received
    sum

  fn in_force(d, period) = not d.revoked and d.first <= period and period <= d.last

  fn per_diem_rate(r) = if r in {Region.Island} then 9000 else if r in {Region.Mainland} then 6000 else 12000

  fn mileage_rate(v) = if v in {Vehicle.Car} then 60 else if v in {Vehicle.Truck} then 90 else 250

  fn add_po_approval(po, who) = po with { approvals: po.approvals ++ [who] }
  fn approve_po(po)           = po with { status enters PoStatus.Approved }
  fn reject_po(po)            = po with { status enters PoStatus.Rejected }
  fn receive_po(po, received) = po with { status enters PoStatus.Received, received: received }
  fn close_po(po)             = po with { status enters PoStatus.Closed }
  fn decide(e, grant, by)     = if grant then e with { status enters ExceptionStatus.Granted, decided_by: by } else e with { status enters ExceptionStatus.Denied, decided_by: by }
  fn match_txn(t, report)     = t with { status enters CardStatus.Matched, matched: report }
  fn dispute_txn(t)           = t with { status enters CardStatus.Disputed }

1	# desk/review.brass
2	module desk.review
3	import desk.ids as ids
4	import desk.lines as lines
5	import desk.staff as staff
6	import desk.reports as reports
7	import desk.audit as audit
8	import desk.host as host
9	import desk.routing as routing
10	import desk.budget as budget
11	
12	interface
13	  fn open_draft(store: host.Store, badge: ids.Badge, period: ids.Period, first_line: lines.Line) -> Outcome<ids.ReportId>
14	  fn add_line(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge, line: lines.Line) -> Outcome<Done>
15	  fn submit(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Done>
16	  fn approve(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, approver: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<reports.ReportStatus>
17	  fn reject(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, approver: ids.Badge, reason: ids.Reason) -> Outcome<Done>
18	  fn request_changes(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, approver: ids.Badge, reason: ids.Reason) -> Outcome<Done>
19	  fn resubmit(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Done>
20	
21	  fn may_act(store: host.Store, r: reports.Submitted, who: staff.Active) -> Outcome<Bool>
22	private
23	  type Gate = { r: reports.Submitted, who: staff.Active }
24	  type Own  = { r: reports.Report, who: staff.Active }
25	
26	  fn gate(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, approver: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Gate>
27	  fn own(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Own>
28	  fn open_and_valid(store: host.Store, r: reports.Report) -> Outcome<Done>
29	  fn required_for(store: host.Store, r: reports.Submitted) -> Outcome<Maybe<ids.Badge>>
30	  fn stand_in(store: host.Store, required: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Maybe<ids.Badge>>
31	  fn final_approval(store: host.Store, r: reports.Submitted, who: staff.Active) -> Outcome<reports.ReportStatus>
32	body
33	  fn open_draft(store, badge, period, first_line) =
34	    let who: staff.Staff = store.staff(badge)?
35	    if who is staff.Active then
36	      let closed: Bool = store.period_closed(period)?
37	      if not closed then
38	        let id: ids.ReportId = store.next_id()?
39	        store.save_report({ id: id, badge: badge, department: who.department, period: period, lines: [first_line], status: reports.ReportStatus.Draft, approvals: [] })?
40	        Ok(id)
41	      else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the period is closed")
42	    else Err(FailureCode.Unauthorized, "staff member is not active")
43	
44	  fn add_line(store, report_id, badge, line) =
45	    let o: Own = own(store, report_id, badge)?
46	    if o.r is reports.Editable then
47	      if o.r.lines.length < 50 then store.save_report(reports.add_line(o.r, line))
48	      else Err(FailureCode.InvalidInput, "a report holds at most 50 lines")
49	    else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the report is not editable")
50	
51	  fn submit(store, report_id, badge) =
52	    let o: Own = own(store, report_id, badge)?
53	    if o.r is reports.Draft then
54	      open_and_valid(store, o.r)?
55	      store.save_report(reports.submit(o.r))?
56	      store.append_audit(audit.entry(badge, o.r.id, reports.ReportStatus.Draft, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, "submitted"))
57	    else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the report is not a draft")
58	
59	  fn resubmit(store, report_id, badge) =
60	    let o: Own = own(store, report_id, badge)?
61	    if o.r is reports.AwaitingChanges then
62	      open_and_valid(store, o.r)?
63	      store.save_report(reports.resubmit(o.r))?
64	      store.append_audit(audit.entry(badge, o.r.id, reports.ReportStatus.ChangesRequested, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, "resubmitted"))
65	    else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the report is not awaiting changes")
66	
67	  fn approve(store, report_id, approver) =
68	    let g: Gate = gate(store, report_id, approver)?
69	    if g.r.approvals.length + 1 >= routing.steps_for(lines.total(g.r.lines)) then final_approval(store, g.r, g.who)
70	    else
71	      store.save_report(reports.add_approval(g.r, g.who.badge))?
72	      store.append_audit(audit.entry(g.who.badge, g.r.id, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, "approved; awaiting the next approver"))?
73	      Ok(reports.ReportStatus.Submitted)
74	
75	  fn reject(store, report_id, approver, reason) =
76	    let g: Gate = gate(store, report_id, approver)?
77	    store.save_report(reports.reject(g.r))?
78	    store.append_audit(audit.entry(g.who.badge, g.r.id, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, reports.ReportStatus.Rejected, reason))
79	
80	  fn request_changes(store, report_id, approver, reason) =
81	    let g: Gate = gate(store, report_id, approver)?
82	    store.save_report(reports.request_changes(g.r))?
83	    store.append_audit(audit.entry(g.who.badge, g.r.id, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, reports.ReportStatus.ChangesRequested, reason))
84	
85	  fn own(store, report_id, badge) =
86	    let who: staff.Staff = store.staff(badge)?
87	    if who is staff.Active then
88	      let r: reports.Report = store.report(report_id)?
89	      if r.badge == badge then Ok({ r: r, who: who })
90	      else Err(FailureCode.Unauthorized, "only the submitter may act on this report")
91	    else Err(FailureCode.Unauthorized, "staff member is not active")
92	
93	  fn open_and_valid(store, r) =
94	    let closed: Bool = store.period_closed(r.period)?
95	    if closed then Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the period is closed")
96	    else if lines.all_valid(r.lines) then Ok(Done)
97	    else Err(FailureCode.InvalidInput, "a line is over its limit or lacks a required receipt")
98	
99	  fn gate(store, report_id, approver) =
100	    let who: staff.Staff = store.staff(approver)?
101	    if who is staff.Active then
102	      let r: reports.Report = store.report(report_id)?
103	      if r is reports.Submitted then
104	        let closed: Bool = store.period_closed(r.period)?
105	        if not closed then
106	          if who.badge != r.badge then
107	            let allowed: Bool = may_act(store, r, who)?
108	            if allowed then Ok({ r: r, who: who })
109	            else Err(FailureCode.Unauthorized, "not this report's next approver")
110	          else Err(FailureCode.Unauthorized, "a report cannot be approved by its submitter")
111	        else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the period is closed")
112	      else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the report is not awaiting approval")
113	    else Err(FailureCode.Unauthorized, "staff member is not active")
114	
115	  fn may_act(store, r, who) =
116	    let required: Maybe<ids.Badge> = required_for(store, r)?
117	    if required == None then Ok(who.role in {ids.Role.Finance})
118	    else Ok(who.badge == required)
119	
120	  fn required_for(store, r) =
121	    let role: ids.Role = routing.role_for(r.approvals.length + 1)
122	    if role in {ids.Role.Finance} then Ok(None)
123	    else if role in {ids.Role.Supervisor} then
124	      let submitter: staff.Staff = store.staff(r.badge)?
125	      if submitter.supervisor != None then stand_in(store, submitter.supervisor)
126	      else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "the submitter has no supervisor")
127	    else
128	      let dept: staff.Department = store.department(r.department)?
129	      stand_in(store, dept.director)
130	
131	  fn stand_in(store, required) =
132	    let person: staff.Staff = store.staff(required)?
133	    if person.active then Ok(required)
134	    else if person.supervisor != None then
135	      let up: staff.Staff = store.staff(person.supervisor)?
136	      if up.active then Ok(person.supervisor)
137	      else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "no active approver stands in for " ++ required)
138	    else Err(FailureCode.Conflict, "no active approver stands in for " ++ required)
139	
140	  fn final_approval(store, r, who) =
141	    let dept: staff.Department = store.department(r.department)?
142	    let others: reports.Reports = store.reports_for(r.department, r.period)?
143	    let within: Bool = budget.spend_of(others) + lines.budgeted_total(r.lines) <= dept.budget
144	    if within or who.role in {ids.Role.Finance} then
145	      let reason: ids.Reason = if within then "approved" else "approved; budget override"
146	      store.save_report(reports.approve(r))?
147	      store.append_audit(audit.entry(who.badge, r.id, reports.ReportStatus.Submitted, reports.ReportStatus.Approved, reason))?
148	      Ok(reports.ReportStatus.Approved)

12	interface
13	  fn open_draft(store: host.Store, badge: ids.Badge, period: ids.Period, first_line: lines.Line) -> Outcome<ids.ReportId>
14	  fn add_line(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge, line: lines.Line) -> Outcome<Done>
15	  fn submit(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Done>

23	  type Gate = { r: reports.Submitted, who: staff.Active }
24	  type Own  = { r: reports.Report, who: staff.Active }

26	  fn gate(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, approver: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Gate>
27	  fn own(store: host.Store, report_id: ids.ReportId, badge: ids.Badge) -> Outcome<Own>
